customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 1: Sources of Information for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: The Importance of a Feasibility Study
customPastQuestions.questionText: What is the importance of a feasibility study?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: It tests business viability, exposes possible operating problems and risks, estimates market demand, identifies production and personnel requirements, and shows how much finance is needed. It supports applications for credit and becomes a blueprint for subsequent business planning. It also helps the entrepreneur anticipate preliminary expenses, working capital, facilities and repayment obligations rather than committing money on guesswork.
keyRubricPoints: Testing business viability and workability before financial commitment
Anticipating capital requirements and operational risks
Supporting commercial loan applications and investor evaluations
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 2; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 1 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 1: Sources of Information for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.questionText: How should an entrepreneur assess whether a new idea has a viable business opportunity?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The entrepreneur should evaluate: (1) Market demand: whether real unsatisfied customer needs exist and buyers are willing and able to pay; (2) Operational workability: whether the technology, materials, and skilled labor can be organized at realistic cost; (3) Economic profitability: whether projected revenues exceed operating expenses and provide adequate return on invested capital; (4) Regulatory and legal environment: statutory compliance, licenses, and environmental requirements; and (5) Founder competence and competitive advantage: whether the entrepreneur possesses the distinctive capabilities to outcompete existing players.
keyRubricPoints: Market demand and willingness to pay
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 2; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 1 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 2: Generating Data for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.questionText: Which information is needed when checking the feasibility of a proposed business venture, and what are the major sources?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Information needed covers: market data (target demographics, consumption patterns, prices of substitutes), technical data (equipment specifications, raw material inputs, power/water requirements), financial data (initial capital outlays, interest rates, unit variable costs), and organizational data (labor wages, legal registration fees).\n\nMajor sources include primary sources (questionnaires, personal interviews with traders and prospective customers, field surveys) and secondary sources (National Bureau of Statistics publications, Central Bank bulletins, trade directories, Chambers of Commerce, and statutory promotional agencies like SMEDAN).
keyRubricPoints: Categories of needed data: market, technical, financial, organizational
Primary sources: questionnaires, field interviews, direct observation
Secondary sources: NBS, CBN, trade associations, SMEDAN
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 3; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 2 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Essential Areas of a Business Plan
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the essential areas of a business plan.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The essential areas of a business plan are: (1) Executive Summary: concise overview of the venture and funding request; (2) Business Description: mission, legal structure, industry classification, and value proposition; (3) Marketing Plan: market analysis, target segment, competitor evaluation, and 4Ps strategy; (4) Operational and Production Plan: facilities, location, equipment, inventory, and supply chain; (5) Management and Organization: organogram, key personnel profiles, and compensation; and (6) Financial Projections: cash flow forecast, profit/loss, balance sheet, break-even analysis, and financing plan.
keyRubricPoints: Management team credentials and organizational structure
Financial projections, cash flow, and break-even
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 4; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 3 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the outline of a business description.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: A business description outline comprises: (1) Registered business name and contact address; (2) Vision and mission statements; (3) Business objectives (short-term and long-term); (4) Form of legal ownership (Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, LLC); (5) Brief history or background of origin; (6) Description of products or services offered; and (7) Unique selling proposition (USP) and competitive positioning within the industry.
keyRubricPoints: Enterprise identity, vision, mission, and objectives
Form of legal ownership and statutory registration
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 3; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 3 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 4: Location or Siting of Business
customPastQuestions.questionText: What questions should be asked when evaluating a possible business location?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Key evaluation questions include: (1) Is the location close to target customers and convenient for them to access? (2) Are essential raw materials and supplies readily available at low freight costs? (3) Is there adequate infrastructure (reliable electrical power, municipal water, telecommunications, road/rail access)? (4) What is the cost, availability, and unionization of local labor? (5) What are the lease costs, property taxes, and municipal development levies? (6) Are there favorable zoning laws and environmental approvals? (7) What is the proximity and aggressive posture of local competitors?
keyRubricPoints: Raw material availability and transport cost
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 5; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 4 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 4: Location or Siting of Business
customPastQuestions.questionText: List and explain important factors in locating a business.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Important location factors include: (1) Nearness to market: minimizes product transit time and finished goods distribution costs; (2) Nearness to raw materials: reduces bulky freight costs for processing industries; (3) Transport facilities: accessibility to all-weather roads, rail lines, and airports; (4) Availability of power and water: continuous industrial electricity and municipal water supplies; (5) Labor supply: pool of skilled, semi-skilled, and managerial personnel; and (6) Government policies: tax holidays, industrial development zones, and environmental regulations.
keyRubricPoints: Proximity to product market versus raw material inputs
Labor pool and municipal government incentives/zoning
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 5; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 4 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Management, Production, and Risk Mitigation Requirements
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the production, marketing, venture, risk-mitigating, and financial management requirements in a business feasibility study.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The requirements are: (1) Production: determining plant capacity, machinery specifications, factory layout, and raw material supply contracts; (2) Marketing: defining target consumer profiles, pricing tactics, distribution channels, and advertising media; (3) Venture management: establishing the legal entity, organogram, board oversight, and executive responsibilities; (4) Risk mitigation: identifying operational, market, and financial risks and designing preventive controls (insurance, safety stock, backup generators); and (5) Financial management: planning capital requirements, managing working capital, monitoring cash flows, and planning debt amortization.
keyRubricPoints: Production planning: throughput capacity, machinery, raw material inputs
Venture governance: legal structure, organizational delegation
Risk mitigation: internal controls, contingency buffers, insurance
Financial control: working capital, cash flows, loan debt service
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 6; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 5 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: How can technical feasibility help a business owner decide whether to produce goods or purchase them?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Technical feasibility resolves make-or-buy decisions by comparing: (1) Cost economics: fixed capital required for machinery, tooling, and plant space versus unit purchase price from outside suppliers; (2) Production volume: whether internal demand is high enough to achieve economies of scale; (3) Quality control: whether outside suppliers can reliably meet strict specifications; (4) Technical competence: whether the enterprise possesses the specialized engineering skills needed to manufacture in-house; and (5) Supplier reliability: vulnerability to supplier price increases, delivery delays, and intellectual property leaks.
keyRubricPoints: Comparative cost analysis: capital expenditure vs supplier unit price
Production scale and break-even volume threshold
Supply chain dependence and risk of supplier opportunism
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 7; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 6 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 7: Defining Management Team for Operation Unit
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Building and Motivating a Reliable Management Team
customPastQuestions.questionText: How can a small business owner build and motivate a reliable management team?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Building the team requires: (1) Writing precise job specifications highlighting required skills and values; (2) Recruiting individuals with complementary capabilities rather than replicating the founder's background; and (3) Verifying references and past performance records.\n\nMotivating the team requires: (1) Offering competitive base compensation with equity-linked incentives (profit-sharing or stock options); (2) Delegating genuine operational authority and empowering autonomous decision-making; (3) Providing professional development and training opportunities; and (4) Establishing transparent performance metrics with timely recognition and feedback.
keyRubricPoints: Delegation of operational authority and empowerment
Continuous training and objective performance appraisals
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 8; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 7 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 8: Market Analysis and Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Measuring Marketing Success and Improving Sales
customPastQuestions.questionText: How may a small business measure marketing success and improve sales performance?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Marketing success is measured using key metrics: (1) Sales volume growth and revenue trends across product lines; (2) Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) compared with Customer Lifetime Value (CLV); (3) Market share expansion relative to competitors; (4) Conversion rates of promotional inquiries into paid orders; and (5) Customer retention and repeat purchase rates.\n\nSales performance can be improved by: (a) Retraining sales representatives on consultative selling; (b) Refining the promotional mix toward higher-converting channels; (c) Introducing customer loyalty rewards; (d) Adjusting pricing or bundling options; and (e) Gathering direct customer feedback to rectify product deficiencies.
keyRubricPoints: Performance metrics: sales growth, CAC vs CLV, market share, conversion rate
Improvement strategies: sales force training, channel optimization, customer loyalty
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 8; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 8 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 8: Market Analysis and Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Definition and Effectiveness of Marketing Plans
customPastQuestions.questionText: What is a marketing plan, and what makes it effective?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: A marketing plan is a comprehensive operational blueprint detailing an organization's market research, target audience segments, competitive positioning, marketing objectives, and specific strategies across the marketing mix (product, price, place, promotion) to generate sales revenue within a specified time horizon.\n\nAn effective marketing plan is characterized by: (1) Grounding in verifiable empirical market research rather than assumptions; (2) Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound (SMART) objectives; (3) Clear definition of target customer profiles and value proposition; (4) Realistic budgeting and ROI targets for promotional campaigns; (5) Actionable implementation timelines with designated personnel accountability; and (6) Built-in monitoring mechanisms and contingency plans.
keyRubricPoints: Comprehensive definition of marketing plan across research, segments, and 4Ps
Six pillars of effectiveness: research grounding, SMART objectives, target clarity, budgeting, accountability, contingency flexibility
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 9; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 8 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 8: Market Analysis and Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Steps in Preparing a Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.questionText: Outline the steps involved in preparing a marketing plan.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The sequential steps are: (1) Environmental scanning and SWOT analysis (identifying internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats); (2) Market research and customer segmentation (defining demographic and geographic target profiles); (3) Establishing quantitative marketing objectives (e.g., target market share, sales volume in units, revenue goals); (4) Formulating the marketing mix strategy (Product features/branding, Pricing strategy, Place/distribution logistics, and Promotional campaigns); (5) Preparing the marketing budget and sales forecast; and (6) Setting up control, tracking, and evaluation mechanisms.
keyRubricPoints: Step 2: Customer segmentation and target definition
Step 5: Budget allocation and sales projection
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 10; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 8 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 8: Market Analysis and Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Controllable Causes of Marketing Plan Failure
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain major controllable causes of failure of a marketing plan.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Controllable causes are internal managerial errors that could have been prevented: (1) Inadequate or biased market research leading to faulty demand assumptions; (2) Unrealistic sales forecasts unsupported by historical data or market capacity; (3) Inappropriate pricing strategy (pricing too high without perceived value or too low to cover overheads); (4) Poor product quality or packaging defects; (5) Ineffective promotional messaging and wrong advertising media selection; (6) Unreliable distribution channels causing frequent stock-outs; and (7) Inadequate marketing budget and poor execution coordination.
keyRubricPoints: Distinction between controllable internal factors vs uncontrollable external shocks
Five key internal failures: faulty research, unrealistic forecasts, flawed pricing, poor distribution, inadequate execution
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 11; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 8 Section 3.3

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain product, price, distribution, promotion, and marketing strategy integration.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Marketing strategy integrates the four Ps into a coherent commercial assault: (1) Product strategy: designing physical features, branding, packaging, warranties, and product differentiation meeting customer needs; (2) Pricing strategy: establishing pricing models (cost-plus, penetration, skimming, psychological) that reflect value and yield margins; (3) Distribution (Place) strategy: selecting direct or indirect intermediary channels, warehousing, and logistics to ensure prompt product delivery; and (4) Promotion strategy: coordinating advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, and public relations.\n\nIntegration ensures that pricing matches product quality and packaging, distribution channels reach the intended demographic, and promotion reinforces the unique brand positioning without conflicting signals.
keyRubricPoints: Comprehensive explanation of each of the 4 Ps
The principle of strategic coherence: aligning price, quality, channels, and communications
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 12; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 9 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: Which factors should influence the price fixed for a new product or service?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Key factors influencing pricing: (1) Total production and operating costs (fixed costs and variable costs providing a pricing floor); (2) Customer price sensitivity and demand elasticity; (3) Competitor pricing benchmarks for substitute offerings; (4) Enterprise marketing objectives (market penetration vs profit maximization); (5) Perceived customer value and brand prestige; and (6) Government regulations, price caps, and statutory taxes (such as VAT).
keyRubricPoints: Customer elasticity and willingness to pay
Strategic launch objectives and regulatory tax context
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 13; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 9 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: How should an entrepreneur market a newly introduced product?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: An entrepreneur should execute a launch strategy: (1) Generate early awareness through high-impact promotional publicity and social media influencer engagement; (2) Offer trial incentives (free product samples, introductory launch discounts, demonstration booths); (3) Secure prominent retail shelf space and distributor buy-in through introductory dealer trade margins; (4) Focus marketing communications on educating consumers about the unique solution the product provides; (5) Solicit rapid customer feedback to make immediate post-launch adjustments; and (6) Provide robust after-sales customer service to drive word-of-mouth recommendations.
keyRubricPoints: Creating awareness through targeted multi-channel promotions
Stimulating initial trial via sampling and introductory pricing
Distributor incentive structuring and shelf placement
Feedback loops and after-sales customer reassurance
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 14; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 9 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: How should a business owner evaluate a proposed change to the business plan during implementation?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: When evaluating proposed changes, management should: (1) Assess impact on strategic objectives: does the adjustment align with the core mission and competitive edge? (2) Conduct financial appraisal: evaluate the additional capital required, impact on cash flow, and revised return on investment; (3) Assess operational disruption: will changing technology or layout cause downtime or compromise quality? (4) Review market response: will customer perception or brand equity be damaged? (5) Evaluate team readiness: does the current staff possess the competencies to execute the altered plan? and (6) Obtain stakeholder consent: notify lenders, partners, and key customers where terms are affected.
keyRubricPoints: Alignment with strategic vision and value proposition
Financial cost-benefit and cash flow impact evaluation
Operational feasibility and execution risk analysis
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 15; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 10 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: What measures help an entrepreneur assess the progress of a business plan during implementation?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Measures include: (1) Milestone Tracking: comparing actual dates against Gantt chart milestone deadlines (e.g., equipment installation, prototype approval); (2) Budget Variance Analysis: checking actual expenditures against budget allocations across departments; (3) Sales Volume vs Targets: monitoring daily and weekly sales against projected forecasts; (4) Cash Burn Rate and Liquidity: tracking actual cash outflow and ensuring bank balances match working capital plans; and (5) Operational Quality Indicators: defect rates, customer complaint logs, and employee turnover.
keyRubricPoints: Milestone deadline tracking against Gantt schedules
Actual sales performance comparison with forecasts
Working capital liquidity and cash flow tracking
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 16; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 10 Section 3.3

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: What financial and other information should a full business plan provide to financial institutions?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Financial institutions require: (1) Total project cost breakdown (capital assets, pre-operational expenses, initial working capital); (2) Proposed financing structure (owner's equity contribution vs loan requested); (3) Projected Cash Flow Statements (monthly for year 1, annually for years 2-3); (4) Projected Pro-Forma Income Statements and Balance Sheets; (5) Break-Even Analysis (BEP units and revenue); (6) Loan amortization schedule and Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR); (7) Pledged collateral valuation and insurance coverage; and (8) Bank statements and audited financial records of promoters.
keyRubricPoints: Total capital cost and financing mix (equity vs debt)
Cash flow forecasts, income statements, and balance sheets
Break-even point and debt service coverage capacity
Collateral documentation and promoter track record
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 17; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 11 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain major components of cash outflows in a venture.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Major cash outflows comprise: (1) Capital expenditures: acquisition of land, factory construction, and machinery purchases; (2) Pre-operational expenses: legal incorporation, licenses, feasibility consulting fees; (3) Operating expenses: raw material purchases, direct labor payroll, utility bills (diesel, electricity, water), factory rent, and packaging; (4) Marketing and administrative overheads: advertising campaigns, sales commissions, insurance premiums, office supplies; (5) Financial charges: loan interest payments and bank service fees; (6) Debt principal repayments; and (7) Taxation and dividend distributions.
keyRubricPoints: Direct operational manufacturing and raw material outflows
Overhead payroll, utility, and administrative disbursements
Debt financing service and statutory tax payments
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 18; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 11 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Internal Sources of Financing: Pros and Cons
customPastQuestions.questionText: How may an entrepreneur obtain funds internally, and what are the advantages and disadvantages?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Internal funding sources include: personal savings, retained business earnings, sale of personal surplus assets, reduction of working capital through tight inventory control, and accelerated collection of accounts receivable.

Advantages: (1) Total independence and retention of 100% equity and control; (2) Zero mandatory debt interest charges or collateral requirements; (3) Quick deployment without lender bureaucracy; and (4) Shows commitment when applying for outside funding later.

Disadvantages: (1) Strictly limited by the personal wealth of the entrepreneur; (2) High personal financial risk in the event of venture failure; and (3) May choke rapid expansion due to insufficient capital depth.
keyRubricPoints: Internal sources: personal savings, retained earnings, asset sales, working capital release
Advantages: control retention, no debt interest burden, rapid availability
Disadvantages: capital scale limitation, personal financial vulnerability
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 19; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 12 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Major Sources of Financing in Nigeria
customPastQuestions.questionText: Mention and discuss major sources for financing a new venture in Nigeria.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Major sources in Nigeria include: (1) Personal savings and bootstrapping; (2) Family and friends (informal soft loans or equity); (3) Commercial bank loans and overdrafts (require collateral and audited records); (4) Trade credit from suppliers (deferring payment for 30-90 days); (5) Microfinance Banks (providing small credit with peer guarantees); (6) Government intervention schemes and Development Finance Institutions (e.g., Bank of Industry, SMEDAN, Central Bank intervention funds); (7) Venture capital and private angel investors; and (8) Equipment leasing companies.
keyRubricPoints: Informal financing: personal savings, family soft capital, trade credit
Institutional lending: commercial banks, microfinance institutions
Development schemes: Bank of Industry, SMEDAN, CBN intervention funds
Equity capital: venture capitalists, angel investors
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 20; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 12 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: State benefits of equipment leasing when financing a new venture.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Benefits of equipment leasing: (1) Conserves critical liquid cash capital by avoiding large upfront capital expenditure outlays; (2) Easier to access than bank loans since the leased equipment acts as its own security; (3) Protects the venture against technological obsolescence (allowing upgrades at lease expiration); (4) Lease rental payments are fully tax-deductible as operating expenses; (5) Flexible payment schedules structured around the seasonal cash generation of the enterprise; and (6) Keeps existing credit lines available for working capital.
keyRubricPoints: Self-securing asset structure without external collateral
Protection against machinery obsolescence and tax deductibility of lease rentals
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 21; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 12 Section 3.3

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Prospective Evaluators of a Business Proposal
customPastQuestions.questionText: Identify the prospective evaluators of a business proposal and what they look for.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Evaluators and their focus areas include: (1) Commercial Banks: focus on debt repayment capacity, cash flow reliability, collateral security, and the 5 Cs of credit; (2) Venture Capitalists and Angel Investors: look for high-growth potential, scalable market size, strong management capability, distinctive intellectual property, and attractive exit strategies; (3) Government and Development Agencies: look for job creation, local raw material utilization, export earnings, and environmental compliance; (4) Trade Suppliers: evaluate creditworthiness and payment promptness before extending credit; and (5) Prospective Partners: seek strategic synergy, shared values, and balanced risk-sharing.
keyRubricPoints: Commercial banks: debt servicing and collateral security
Venture capitalists: market scalability, ROI, management quality, exit horizon
Government agencies: socioeconomic impact, employment, foreign exchange
Trade partners: credit risk and strategic alignment
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 23; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 13 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Introductory Page of a Business Proposal
customPastQuestions.questionText: Discuss the introductory page component of a business proposal.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The introductory (title) page provides the formal front cover and identification of the proposal: (1) Company name and registered trade logo; (2) Clear, descriptive title of the proposal; (3) Names, titles, and professional contact details of promoters; (4) Name and address of the institution/individual to whom it is submitted; (5) Date of publication and version control; and (6) Legal confidentiality notice or Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) clause stating proprietary rights.
keyRubricPoints: Corporate name, contact information, and logo
Clear project title and recipient identification
Date, version number, and confidentiality/NDA disclaimer
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 24; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 13 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.questionText: What should be included in a complete business proposal beyond the financial statements?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Beyond financial statements, a complete proposal must include: (1) Executive summary and company profile; (2) Comprehensive market analysis and competitor profiling; (3) Detailed marketing strategy (4 Ps); (4) Technical specifications, machinery layout, and production process flowcharts; (5) Management organogram, resumes of key executives, and advisory board profiles; (6) Risk analysis and mitigation strategies; (7) Implementation timeline (Gantt chart milestones); and (8) Appendices containing statutory certificates (CAC incorporation, NAFDAC, environmental impact permits, lease agreements, and letters of intent from major buyers).
keyRubricPoints: Market research and competitive positioning documentation
Technical manufacturing flows and engineering drawings
Statutory compliance licenses, permits, and supplier agreements
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 25; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 13 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Recording Cash Outflows in Cash Flow Statements
customPastQuestions.questionText: What cash outflows should be recorded in a projected cash flow statement?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Cash outflows recorded across operating, investing, and financing activities include: (1) Cash purchases of raw materials and inventory; (2) Payments to accounts payable trade creditors; (3) Factory wages and administrative executive salaries; (4) Utility bills, generator fuel, and rent payments; (5) Marketing and promotional campaign expenses; (6) Capital expenditures on plant, machinery, and vehicles; (7) Bank loan interest charges and loan principal amortization payments; and (8) Corporate income taxes and statutory dues.
keyRubricPoints: Operating payments: raw materials, wages, rent, utilities, marketing
Investing outflows: machinery and capital asset acquisitions
Financing outflows: debt interest and principal repayments, tax disbursements
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 26; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 14 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Payback Period vs Accounting Rate of Return
customPastQuestions.session: POP Appraisal Revision Q1
customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate the payback period and the accounting rate of return (ARR) methods of investment appraisal.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The Payback Period measures the exact time (years/months) required for the undiscounted cumulative net cash inflows of an investment to equal its initial cash outlay. It emphasizes capital liquidity and risk minimization.

In contrast, the Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) measures the ratio of the projected average annual accounting net profit (after depreciation and taxes) to the average investment (or initial capital outlay) expressed as a percentage: ARR = (Average Annual Net Profit / Average Investment) × 100%.

Key differences: (1) Payback uses cash flows; ARR uses accounting profits; (2) Payback focuses on liquidity and project speed; ARR focuses on accounting profitability; (3) Both share the critical flaw of ignoring the Time Value of Money.
keyRubricPoints: Payback definition: time required to recover initial cash investment
ARR formula: Average Annual Accounting Profit / Average Investment * 100
Cash flow basis vs accounting profit basis
Shared limitation: neglect of the Time Value of Money
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 28; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 15 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 16: Discounted Cash Flow Methods of Appraisal
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Comprehensive NPV Calculation and Project Recommendation
customPastQuestions.questionText: A project costs N2,000,000 and yields N800,000, N900,000, N1,000,000, and N600,000 in Years 1 to 4 respectively. At a 12% discount rate, calculate the Net Present Value (NPV) and advise management on project acceptance.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
NPV Calculation Table (Discount rate r = 12%):

Year 0: Outflow (N2,000,000) × 1.0000 = (N2,000,000.00)
Year 1: Inflow N800,000 × 0.8929 = N714,320.00
Year 2: Inflow N900,000 × 0.7972 = N717,480.00
Year 3: Inflow N1,000,000 × 0.7118 = N711,800.00
Year 4: Inflow N600,000 × 0.6355 = N381,300.00

Total Present Value of Cash Inflows = N714,320 + N717,480 + N711,800 + N381,300 = N2,524,900.00

NPV = Total PV of Inflows - Initial Outlay = N2,524,900.00 - N2,000,000.00 = +N524,900.00.

Management Advice: Since the Net Present Value is positive (+N524,900.00), the project generates returns superior to the 12% cost of capital and adds N524,900 to the total wealth of the owners. Management is advised to ACCEPT the project.

workedSolutionSteps.description: Sum Present Values and Subtract Initial Capital Cost

keyRubricPoints: Accurate individual annual present value computations
Definitive acceptance recommendation based on positive NPV rule
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 29; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 16 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 16: Discounted Cash Flow Methods of Appraisal
customPastQuestions.session: POP Appraisal Revision Q2
customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Net Present Value (NPV) discounts all cash flows at the enterprise's specified hurdle rate (cost of capital) and calculates the absolute net currency surplus (in Naira) added to enterprise wealth.

Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the specific break-even discount rate that equates the present value of future cash inflows exactly to the initial capital outlay (making NPV = 0). It represents an internal percentage yield.

Key differences: (1) Measurement unit: NPV is expressed in absolute currency; IRR is expressed as a percentage rate; (2) Reinvestment assumption: NPV assumes intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the realistic cost of capital, whereas IRR unrealistically assumes reinvestment at the internal rate of return; (3) Mutually exclusive choices: NPV is technically superior because it directly maximizes shareholder monetary wealth.
keyRubricPoints: NPV: absolute monetary addition to shareholder wealth discounted at cost of capital
IRR: percentage discount rate where NPV equals zero
Theoretical superiority of NPV in mutually exclusive selections
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 31; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 16 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 17: Economic Appraisal and Evaluation of Projects
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Scope and Nature of Economic Analysis
customPastQuestions.questionText: What sorts of questions does economic analysis try to answer?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Economic analysis asks whether the project uses scarce national resources efficiently; whether the overall social benefits justify economic costs; what wider gains or losses arise for the community; how alternative projects compare; whether market prices reflect true resource costs; what corrections are needed for taxes, subsidies and other transfers; and how the project affects employment, connected activities and national output. It seeks a public-economy judgement that can differ from the private investor's profitability calculation.
keyRubricPoints: Efficient utilization of scarce national resources
Net social benefits and externalities generated for the wider community
Adjusting market prices for distortionary taxes, duties, and subsidies (transfer payments)
Employment generation and national output contribution vs private financial profit
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 35; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 17 Section 3.1.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 17: Economic Appraisal and Evaluation of Projects
customPastQuestions.questionText: What are the two types of linkage effects of a project?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Backward linkages are additional activities and demand created among suppliers of inputs needed by a new project, such as transport, building materials, agricultural products or service providers supplying the venture. Forward linkages arise when the project's output provides an input or creates opportunities for other activities that use it. For example, a newly established institution may stimulate nearby accommodation, restaurants and other services, while a processing enterprise can create downstream users of its output. Linkages show how a project can affect other sectors beyond its own direct costs and revenue.
keyRubricPoints: Backward linkages: stimulated demand for input suppliers (raw materials, transport, construction)
Forward linkages: output creates downstream utilization opportunities for other enterprises
Concrete example: polytechnic/institution stimulating private hostels, dining, hair salons
Significance in economic versus private financial appraisal
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: PSALMDATA Past Question Document, Page 36; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 17 Section 3.1.4

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 1: Sources of Information for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Pre-feasibility vs Detailed Study & Information Sources
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q1
customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between a pre-feasibility study and a comprehensive feasibility study, and identify three primary and three secondary sources of data used in feasibility investigations in Nigeria.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
A pre-feasibility study is an initial, exploratory evaluation designed to quickly screen an entrepreneurial idea to determine whether it warrants the substantial time and expenditure of a complete investigation. In contrast, a comprehensive feasibility study is a rigorous, detailed, and exhaustive appraisal of the venture's technical, financial, commercial, and operational viability before committing capital.

Primary data sources in Nigeria include: (1) Direct surveys of potential consumers using questionnaires; (2) In-depth interviews with distributors, wholesalers, and retailers; and (3) Observational traffic counts and competitive mystery shopping.

Secondary data sources include: (1) National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) demographic and trade publications; (2) Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) statistical bulletins and interest rate bulletins; and (3) Publications of statutory promotional agencies such as SMEDAN, NDE, and Chambers of Commerce (LCCI/NACCIMA).
customPastQuestions.modelAnswer: Pre-feasibility serves as preliminary screening; full feasibility provides exhaustive operational and financial verification. Primary sources include surveys, interviews, and direct observations. Secondary sources include NBS, CBN, SMEDAN, and trade associations.
keyRubricPoints: Accurate contrast between preliminary screening (pre-feasibility) and exhaustive viability assessment (full study)
Three authentic primary sources: consumer questionnaires, distributor interviews, direct field observation
Three authentic Nigerian secondary sources: NBS, CBN, SMEDAN/Chambers of Commerce
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 3; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 1 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 2: Generating Data for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Primary Data Gathering and Non-Response Bias
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q2
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the structured questionnaire and personal interview methods for gathering market data during feasibility research. What practical measures should an investigator take to minimize non-response bias?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Structured questionnaires use predetermined, sequenced questions (closed-ended and open-ended) to collect standardized quantitative data from a broad sample of respondents efficiently. Personal interviews involve face-to-face dialogue that allows deep probing, immediate clarification of complex queries, and qualitative insight into buyer motivation.

To minimize non-response bias: (1) Keep the questionnaire concise and focused on essential variables; (2) Pre-test the research instrument for ambiguity; (3) Offer non-coercive incentives or professional courtesy explanations; (4) Follow up with non-respondents across multiple communication channels; and (5) Train field enumerators to establish polite rapport and guarantee confidentiality.
keyRubricPoints: Structured questionnaire characteristics: standardization, wide reach, closed vs open questions
Personal interview characteristics: probing, flexibility, high response rate, higher cost
Non-response reduction measures: concise wording, pilot pre-testing, respectful follow-up, assured confidentiality
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 6; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 2 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Business Description Elements and Legal Structure
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q3
customPastQuestions.questionText: Detail the critical elements required in the business description section of a feasibility report, highlighting why defining the enterprise's legal form of ownership (Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, Limited Liability Company) is fundamental to feasibility.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The business description must encompass: (1) Enterprise name, mission, vision, and core values; (2) Nature of business, sector, and industry classification; (3) Distinctive value proposition and product/service portfolio; (4) Growth history or inception background; (5) Ownership and legal form of registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC); and (6) Current status and competitive advantage.

Specifying the legal structure is critical because it dictates: (a) Liability exposure of the founders (unlimited personal liability in sole proprietorship/general partnership vs limited liability in LLC); (b) Ability to attract outside debt and equity capital; (c) Tax obligations and statutory compliance requirements under the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA); and (d) Business continuity and perpetual succession upon the death or exit of a founder.
keyRubricPoints: Six essential elements: name/mission, industry classification, product line, inception, legal form, competitive advantage
Liability implications: personal asset vulnerability vs limited corporate shield
Capital access and investor eligibility under CAMA regulations
Perpetual succession and corporate governance continuity
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 9; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 3 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 4: Location or Siting of Business
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Plant Location vs Retail Siting Criteria
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q4
customPastQuestions.questionText: Distinguish between plant location factors for a manufacturing enterprise and site location factors for a consumer retail business according to ENT 302 principles.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Manufacturing plant location prioritizes cost minimization, logistics efficiency, and regulatory compliance: (1) Proximity to heavy raw materials (especially where materials are bulky or weight-losing); (2) Availability of reliable industrial power, water, and waste disposal; (3) Access to freight transport arteries (rail, highways, ports); (4) Cost and supply of technical and semi-skilled labor; and (5) Local zoning and environmental protection laws.

In contrast, consumer retail siting is revenue and convenience-driven: (1) Pedestrian foot traffic density and vehicular visibility; (2) Proximity and accessibility to target demographic clusters; (3) Parking convenience and ingress/egress safety; (4) Neighboring tenant synergy and compatible commercial draws; and (5) Lease terms and rent per square meter.
keyRubricPoints: Manufacturing focus: input cost minimization, bulk raw material proximity, industrial infrastructure, freight
Retail focus: customer foot-traffic, visibility, accessibility, demographic purchasing power, parking
Reference to Weberian location principles and NOUN ENT 302 Unit 4 guidelines
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 13; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 4 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q5
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain how management organizational structuring and production planning interact in a new enterprise. Outline the key considerations for determining production capacity and raw material inventory control.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Management structuring creates the division of labor, reporting hierarchy, and supervisory controls necessary to execute the production schedule seamlessly. Without clear delegation, production bottlenecks, wastage, and safety violations escalate.

Key considerations for production capacity: (1) Projected market demand and seasonal peak fluctuations; (2) Rated machine capacity versus realistic effective operating hours; and (3) Availability and downtime for maintenance.

Key considerations for raw materials inventory control: (1) Lead times required by domestic and foreign suppliers; (2) Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) balancing ordering costs against carrying costs; (3) Safety stock margins to prevent stock-outs during logistics disruptions; and (4) Perishability and warehouse storage conditions.
keyRubricPoints: Interaction between organogram/delegation and factory floor execution
Determining capacity: market demand, machine throughput, maintenance downtime
Inventory control variables: supplier lead time, holding vs ordering costs, safety stock buffer
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 16; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 5 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Technical Feasibility and Machinery Selection Criteria
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q6
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the scope of technical analysis in a feasibility report. What criteria should guide the entrepreneur in selecting plant equipment, machinery, and production technology?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Technical analysis assesses the physical, engineering, and manufacturing feasibility of the project. It examines whether the product can be produced at acceptable quality standards, within cost budgets, and using proven technology.

Criteria for selecting machinery and technology: (1) Technical suitability and capacity alignment with market demand; (2) Ease of operation and availability of local technical personnel to maintain it; (3) Availability and cost of spare parts locally; (4) Energy efficiency and compatibility with local power supply; (5) Obsolescence risk and flexibility to adapt to future product changes; and (6) Capital acquisition cost versus warranty and supplier after-sales support.
keyRubricPoints: Scope of technical analysis: physical feasibility, engineering specifications, site layout
Selection criteria: throughput capacity, local maintenance expertise, spare parts availability
Energy requirements, technology obsolescence risk, and vendor support
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 19; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 6 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 7: Defining Management Team for Operation Unit
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Management Team Credentials and Investor Scrutiny
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q7
customPastQuestions.questionText: Why do financial institutions and investors scrutinize the background, technical qualifications, and track record of the management team when evaluating a feasibility proposal?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Venture capitalists and commercial lenders recognize that a brilliant business idea with mediocre management frequently fails, whereas an experienced, cohesive management team can navigate market uncertainties and execute successfully. Evaluators scrutinize: (1) Relevant industry experience and technical expertise; (2) Complementary skill sets spanning finance, marketing, operations, and leadership; (3) Past managerial track record and integrity; (4) Commitment to the venture (including personal financial equity stake); and (5) Succession planning and key-man insurance to mitigate reliance on a single individual.
keyRubricPoints: Investor adage: backing the jockey (management) over the horse (idea)
Scrutiny dimensions: industry track record, complementary functional skills, personal equity commitment
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 22; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 7 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 8: Market Analysis and Marketing Plan
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Market Segmentation and Total Addressable Market Sizing
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q8
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the four bases of market segmentation (geographic, demographic, psychographic, and behavioral) and explain how an entrepreneur calculates Total Addressable Market (TAM) and market share in feasibility planning.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The four bases of segmentation are: (1) Geographic: location, urban/rural density, climate, state/region; (2) Demographic: age, gender, household income, education, occupation; (3) Psychographic: lifestyle, social class, values, personal aspirations; and (4) Behavioral: usage frequency, brand loyalty, purchase readiness, price sensitivity.

Calculating TAM and Market Share: TAM is the total annual market demand or revenue potential if 100% of the target population purchased the product (Total Target Customers × Average Annual Consumption × Unit Price). Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM) is the portion reachable by the enterprise's channels. Projected Market Share is the percentage of SAM the new firm realistically captures within 1 to 3 years based on production capacity, competitor strength, and marketing expenditure.
keyRubricPoints: Detailed breakdown of all four segmentation criteria with practical examples
Formulaic and conceptual derivation of Total Addressable Market (TAM)
Realistic market share estimation factoring production constraints and competitors
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 25; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 8 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Price Penetration vs Price Skimming Strategies
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q9
customPastQuestions.questionText: Evaluate price penetration versus price skimming strategies for a newly introduced product. In what market conditions is each pricing strategy recommended?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Price Penetration sets an initially low price to attract high sales volume rapidly, deter competitors, and capture dominant market share. It is recommended when: (1) Market demand is price elastic (highly sensitive to price); (2) Economies of scale can be achieved quickly at high production volumes; and (3) Intense competition threatens fast follower entry.

Price Skimming sets an initially premium price to recover heavy R&D and launch costs from less price-sensitive early adopters before lowering prices systematically. It is recommended when: (1) The product has high perceived prestige, distinctive uniqueness, or patent protection; (2) Demand is inelastic; (3) Production capacity is initially limited; and (4) Competitors cannot enter the market immediately.
keyRubricPoints: Price Penetration: low entry price, mass volume, high price elasticity, scale economies
Price Skimming: premium entry price, margin recovery, unique value/patents, low price elasticity
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 28; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 9 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Gantt Charts and Implementation Risk Mitigation
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q10
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the role of the Gantt chart and milestone scheduling in business plan implementation. What operational risks cause delays in project execution?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
A Gantt chart visually maps project activities, their start dates, durations, task dependencies, and scheduled completion milestones along a calendar timeline. It enables management to identify the critical path, allocate physical and financial resources synchronously, and monitor variance between planned and actual progress.

Operational risks causing execution delays include: (1) Delays in statutory approvals, environmental permits, and CAC registration; (2) Machinery procurement, shipping customs bottlenecks, and port clearing delays; (3) Construction cost overruns and building contractor non-performance; (4) Key personnel recruitment and training shortfalls; and (5) Working capital cash deficits resulting from delayed loan disbursements.
keyRubricPoints: Gantt chart functionality: visual timeline, activity dependencies, critical path, variance monitoring
Key milestone markers: CAC incorporation, site acquisition, machine commissioning, commercial launch
Operational delay risks: regulatory approvals, customs/shipping, contractor defaults, cash flow timing
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 31; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 10 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Break-Even Point (BEP) and Margin of Safety Numerical Analysis
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q11
customPastQuestions.questionText: Define Break-Even Point (BEP). Given that a firm has fixed costs of N1,200,000, variable cost per unit of N400, and selling price per unit of N700, calculate: (i) Break-even volume in units, (ii) Break-even revenue in Naira, and (iii) Margin of safety if anticipated sales are 6,000 units.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Break-Even Point (BEP) is the level of operations where total revenue exactly equals total costs, yielding neither profit nor loss.

Formulae & Calculations:
Contribution margin per unit (CM) = Selling Price (P) - Variable Cost per unit (VC) = N700 - N400 = N300.

(i) BEP (units) = Fixed Costs / CM = N1,200,000 / N300 = 4,000 units.

(ii) BEP (revenue) = BEP (units) × Selling Price = 4,000 × N700 = N2,800,000.
Alternatively: FC / (CM / P) = N1,200,000 / (300 / 700) = N2,800,000.

(iii) Margin of Safety:
In units = Budgeted Sales - BEP Sales = 6,000 - 4,000 = 2,000 units.
In value = 2,000 × N700 = N1,400,000.
In percentage = (Budgeted Sales - BEP Sales) / Budgeted Sales = (6,000 - 4,000) / 6,000 × 100% = 33.33%.

workedSolutionSteps.description: Calculate BEP Volume in Units (FC / CM)

keyRubricPoints: Formal definition of Break-Even Point as zero-profit threshold
Step 1: Unit contribution margin of N300
Step 2: Correct BEP volume of 4,000 units
Step 3: Correct BEP sales revenue of N2,800,000
Step 4: Margin of safety: 2,000 units, N1,400,000, or 33.33%
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 34; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 11 Section 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Debt vs Equity Financing and the 5 Cs of Credit
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q12
customPastQuestions.questionText: Compare debt financing and equity financing in capital structuring for a new venture. Explain the '5 Cs of Credit' used by commercial bankers to assess loan applications.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Debt financing involves borrowed capital that must be repaid with interest according to a contractual amortization schedule, regardless of profitability, but does not dilute voting ownership. Equity financing involves issuing ownership shares in exchange for permanent capital without mandatory interest obligations, but dilutes control and entitles investors to residual profits.

The 5 Cs of Credit evaluated by commercial banks are: (1) Character: the borrower's reputation, integrity, and credit history; (2) Capacity: cash flow generation ability to comfortably service debt repayments; (3) Capital: the founder's personal equity invested in the venture (skin in the game); (4) Collateral: pledgeable assets securing the loan in case of default; and (5) Conditions: macroeconomic environment, interest rate trends, and industry viability.
keyRubricPoints: Debt vs Equity contrast: interest obligation vs ownership dilution, bankruptcy risk vs control
Character: borrower integrity and track record
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 37; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 12 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q13
customPastQuestions.questionText: What is an Executive Summary, and why is it often considered the single most critical section of a business proposal presented to prospective investors?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
The Executive Summary is a concise, high-level synthesis of the entire business proposal, typically spanning 1 to 2 pages, capturing the business model, target market, competitive edge, management team qualifications, capital funding requirement, and financial return forecasts.

It is the most critical section because: (1) It is the first (and sometimes only) section busy loan officers and angel investors read; (2) It serves as a gateway filter determining whether the reader commits time to review the complete proposal; (3) It articulates the venture's core investment thesis and value proposition succinctly; and (4) It showcases managerial clarity and commercial professionalism.
keyRubricPoints: Definition of Executive Summary as 1-2 page synthesis of business model and returns
Gateway filter role: decisive factor in whether investors read further
Key components included: concept, problem solved, team, financing sought, expected ROI
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 40; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 13 Section 3.1

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Net Profit vs Net Cash Flow and Insolvency Dynamics
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q14
customPastQuestions.questionText: Distinguish between accounting net profit and net cash flow. Why is a profitable enterprise still vulnerable to insolvency if cash flow forecasting is poorly managed?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Accounting net profit is computed on an accrual basis (Revenue earned minus Expenses incurred), recording revenue at the point of sale whether cash has been received or not, and recognizing non-cash deductions such as depreciation. Net cash flow measures actual liquid money received minus liquid money disbursed during the accounting period.

A business can be highly profitable on paper yet collapse into technical insolvency if: (1) Substantial revenues are locked up in uncollected accounts receivable (credit sales); (2) High cash outlays are required upfront for inventory and raw materials before sales occur; (3) Heavy debt principal repayments must be serviced (which do not appear on the income statement as expenses); and (4) Large capital expenditure commitments exhaust cash reserves.
keyRubricPoints: Accrual accounting basis (profit) versus liquidity timing (cash flow)
Non-cash items (depreciation) and balance sheet movements (principal repayment)
Four causes of profitable failure: credit customer delays, inventory buildup, debt principal drain, capital expenditures
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 42; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 14 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Payback Period Calculation and Traditional Method Limitations
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q15
customPastQuestions.questionText: An investment requires an initial cash outlay of N5,000,000 and generates annual net cash inflows of N1,500,000, N2,000,000, N1,800,000, and N1,200,000 over four years. Calculate the Payback Period, and discuss two major limitations of the traditional payback method.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Cumulative cash flow schedule:
Year 0: (N5,000,000)
Year 1 inflow: N1,500,000 -> Cumulative recovered: N1,500,000 (Remaining: N3,500,000)
Year 2 inflow: N2,000,000 -> Cumulative recovered: N3,500,000 (Remaining: N1,500,000)
Year 3 inflow: N1,800,000 -> Inflow exceeds required N1,500,000.
Fraction of Year 3 needed = N1,500,000 / N1,800,000 = 0.833 years.
Payback Period = 2 years + 0.833 years = 2.83 years (approximately 2 years and 10 months).

Two major limitations:
(1) Ignores the Time Value of Money: It treats N1 received in Year 4 equally to N1 received in Year 1 without discounting for inflation or cost of capital.
(2) Ignores cash flows occurring after the payback threshold: A project that yields massive profits in Year 4 and 5 could be rejected in favor of a project that breaks even slightly earlier but yields nothing thereafter.

workedSolutionSteps.description: Compute Cumulative Cash Flows for Years 1 & 2

keyRubricPoints: Accurate cumulative cash flow calculation for Years 1 and 2
Final answer: 2.83 years or 2 years 10 months
Limitation 1: Neglects Time Value of Money
Limitation 2: Ignores cash flows beyond the cut-off payback date
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 44; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 15 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 16: Discounted Cash Flow Methods of Appraisal
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Discounted Cash Flow Decision Rules and NPV vs IRR Conflicts
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q16
customPastQuestions.questionText: State the decision rules for Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and Profitability Index (PI). In the event of conflicting rankings between NPV and IRR for mutually exclusive projects, which criterion should the financial analyst prioritize and why?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Decision Rules:
(1) Net Present Value (NPV): Accept if NPV > 0; Reject if NPV < 0; Indifferent if NPV = 0.
(2) Internal Rate of Return (IRR): Accept if IRR > Cost of Capital (r); Reject if IRR < r.
(3) Profitability Index (PI): Accept if PI > 1.0; Reject if PI < 1.0.

Conflicting Rankings: For mutually exclusive projects with differing cash flow timings or unequal scales of investment, NPV and IRR may give conflicting rankings. The financial analyst must prioritize NPV. NPV measures the absolute net addition to total shareholder wealth in currency value (Naira), whereas IRR is a relative percentage rate that implicitly assumes cash inflows are reinvested at the internal rate of return rather than the enterprise's realistic cost of capital.
keyRubricPoints: Formal acceptance criteria for NPV (>0), IRR (>r), and PI (>1)
Identification of reasons for conflict: scale differences and reinvestment rate assumptions
Superiority of NPV based on shareholder wealth maximization
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 46; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 16 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 17: Economic Appraisal and Evaluation of Projects
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Social Cost-Benefit Analysis and Shadow Pricing
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q17
customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the rationale for Social Cost-Benefit Analysis (SCBA) in public-private project appraisal. What are shadow prices, and why must market prices of labor and foreign currency be adjusted in developing economies like Nigeria?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer:
Social Cost-Benefit Analysis (SCBA) assesses a project from the perspective of the entire society and national economy rather than the narrow commercial profitability of private shareholders. It evaluates whether the project contributes net social welfare, generates employment, saves foreign exchange, and creates backward/forward economic linkages.

Shadow prices represent the true social opportunity cost of economic resources when prevailing market prices are distorted by taxes, subsidies, import tariffs, price controls, or monopolistic practices.

Adjustments in developing economies like Nigeria:
(1) Shadow Wage Rate for Unskilled Labor: In an economy with widespread underemployment, the market minimum wage exceeds the true opportunity cost of labor (foregone agricultural output). Shadow wages reflect this lower opportunity cost.
(2) Shadow Exchange Rate: Official foreign exchange rates often overvalue local currency due to import rationing, so foreign currency saved or spent must be valued at its true scarcity value (shadow exchange rate) to prevent distorted project selection.
keyRubricPoints: Distinction between private commercial profitability and national social welfare
Definition of shadow price as true economic opportunity cost adjusting for market distortions
Shadow wage rate rationale under structural unemployment
Shadow foreign exchange rate rationale under foreign exchange scarcity
customPastQuestions.sourceReference: ENT 302 Summary Guide, Page 48; NOUN ENT 302 Unit 17 Section 3.1 & 3.2

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 1: Sources of Information for Feasibility Studies
customPastQuestions.topicTitle: Statutory Regulatory Bodies in Nigerian Feasibility Investigations
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q18
options: A. Only the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)
B. NBS, NDE, SMEDAN, Ministries of Commerce, and Chambers of Commerce
C. International Monetary Fund and World Bank headquarters exclusively
D. State police commands and federal road safety commissions

customPastQuestions.questionText: Which of the following groups constitutes the primary statutory and governmental data sources for conducting feasibility studies in Nigeria according to ENT 302?

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q19
customPastQuestions.questionText: What is a Unique Selling Proposition (USP) in the context of the business description, and how does it differentiate a new venture from established market incumbents?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: A Unique Selling Proposition (USP) is the distinctive factor or benefit that clearly distinguishes a company's product or service from its competitors. It articulates why customers should choose this enterprise over alternatives. customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning

customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q20
customPastQuestions.questionText: Outline the steps involved in constructing a Competitor Profiling Matrix during market feasibility analysis.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Steps to construct a Competitor Profiling Matrix: (1) Identify direct, indirect, and future substitute competitors in the target market; (2) Determine key success factors (KSFs) in the industry (e.g., pricing, product quality, brand reputation, distribution reach, customer service); (3) Assign weighting to each success factor according to market significance; (4) Rate each competitor and the new venture against these factors on a standardized scale (1 to 5); and (5) Calculate composite scores to reveal competitive vulnerabilities and strategic opportunities.
keyRubricPoints: Identification of direct, indirect, and substitute competitors

customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q21
customPastQuestions.questionText: Compare direct marketing channels (manufacturer to consumer) with indirect channels (wholesalers and retailers) in the Nigerian business environment.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Direct channels allow total control over brand presentation, customer relationships, pricing margins, and immediate feedback, but demand heavy capital expenditure in logistics, retail outlets, or digital fulfillment. Indirect channels leverage established distribution networks, warehousing, and local market reach of wholesalers and retailers, reducing initial capital outlays, but sacrifice profit margins and weaken direct connection with end users.

customPastQuestions.questionText: Explain the role of Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) like the Bank of Industry (BOI) in providing concessionary long-term credit to small and medium manufacturing enterprises in Nigeria.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Development Finance Institutions provide concessionary, long-term single-digit interest rate loans and equipment leasing facilities tailored for industrial transformation, filling the funding gap left by commercial banks which prefer short-term, double-digit rate commercial trading loans. customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Feasibility and Business Planning
customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 16: Discounted Cash Flow Methods of Appraisal
customPastQuestions.session: Summary & TMA Review Q24
customPastQuestions.questionText: State the Profitability Index (Benefit-Cost Ratio) formula and explain how it resolves capital rationing when an entrepreneur has multiple positive NPV projects but limited capital.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Profitability Index (PI) = Present Value of Future Cash Inflows / Initial Cash Outlay = PV / I0. In capital rationing where capital is constrained, ranking projects by absolute NPV can be suboptimal because large projects absorb all capital while yielding lower return per Naira invested. Ranking by Profitability Index identifies the combination of projects that generates the highest total net present value per unit of constrained capital.
keyRubricPoints: PI formula: PV of Cash Inflows / Initial Outlay
Capital rationing principle: maximizing return per Naira of restricted investment capital

customPastQuestions.linkedUnitTitle: Unit 11: Corporate Governance and Board of Directors
customPastQuestions.questionText: Enumerate the major sources of power in an organization and explain any four.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: French and Raven distinguish five bases: legitimate power comes from formal office; reward power from the ability to provide valued benefits; coercive power from the capacity to punish non-compliance; referent power from admiration and followers' desire to identify with the leader; and expert power from recognised knowledge and skill. For example, an appointed director may possess legitimate power, while a highly respected technical specialist exercises expert power. Effective leadership relies on appropriate use of these powers rather than fear alone.

customPastQuestions.courseTitle: Leadership and Corporate Governance
customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between the Functional or Group Approach and Action-Centered Leadership.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: The functional or group approach defines leadership by the functions necessary for a group to work effectively, rather than by the leader's birth, personality or job title. Leadership skills can therefore be learnt and improved. John Adair's action-centred leadership develops this approach into three overlapping needs: achieving the task, maintaining the team and meeting each individual member's needs. The broad functional approach asks what leadership contributes to a group; Adair specifies the three interdependent areas that the leader must balance.

customPastQuestions.questionText: What do you understand by transactional leadership theory?
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Transactional leadership rests on a clear exchange between leader and followers. Unlike transformational leadership, the central emphasis is normally meeting established objectives rather than altering followers' values and aspirations.

customPastQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between limitations and delimitations in research.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Delimitations are intentional boundaries imposed by the researcher to make the study specific and manageable: choosing a particular study centre, limiting the period to one semester or investigating only 300-level students. customPastQuestions.questionText: Hypotheses are regarded as tentative answers to research problems. They are usually expressed in the form of a relationship between independent and dependent variables. Expatiate on research hypotheses and its characteristics with examples.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: A research hypothesis is a provisional, testable explanation or prediction offered as a possible answer to a research problem. It usually states an expected relation between variables, thereby guiding the data required and its analysis. A good hypothesis is clear, specific, logically grounded, relevant, measurable or otherwise testable, and open to confirmation or rejection by evidence. Example: 'Increased funding improves the quality of hotel services' connects funding (independent variable) with service quality (dependent variable). Its null form is: 'There is no significant relationship between funding and service quality.' A hypothesis is not a final conclusion.

First, select a person, institution or situation and clarify why it requires investigation. Carry out a second, more focused round of data gathering, cross-check accounts and interpret the evidence as a whole. Where the purpose is remedial, propose or test appropriate alternative measures. The final account should preserve confidentiality, explain the case coherently and avoid claiming wider generalisation unsupported by the evidence.

customPastQuestions.questionText: Define Experimental Research and discuss its main characteristics; briefly explain the concept and three characteristics of experimental research.
customPastQuestions.suppliedAnswer: Experimental research is systematic investigation of a possible cause-and-effect relationship by deliberately varying an independent variable and observing an outcome while other relevant conditions are controlled. Its three principal characteristics are control (hold constant or minimise influences outside the treatment), manipulation (introduce different treatment conditions) and observation (measure responses or dependent-variable changes after the treatment). For example, a researcher may compare customer-service performance after two different staff-training arrangements, while controlling relevant conditions. Strong experiments also describe their participants, instruments and method of comparison clearly.
